points_json.example: A woman whose heart races at 150 beats per minute for no reason, convinced she is having a heart attack — emergency tests show nothing wrong.
points_json.point: A panic attack is a sudden surge of intense fear that peaks within minutes. DSM-5-TR lists 13 symptoms: racing heart, sweating, trembling, shortness of breath, choking feeling, chest pain, nausea, dizziness, chills or heat, numbness, feeling unreal, fear of losing control, and fear of dying. Four or more of these make a full attack.

points_json.example: A man who had a panic attack in a shopping mall now avoids all malls, cinemas, and crowded markets, fearing another attack.
points_json.point: Panic Disorder means repeated, unexpected panic attacks plus at least one month of worry about more attacks or major behavior change to avoid them. The attacks must not be caused by drugs, medical conditions, or another mental disorder.

points_json.example: A student who misreads a normal fast heartbeat after climbing stairs as proof that she is dying.
points_json.point: The cognitive model says panic grows from catastrophic misinterpretation of body sensations. A racing heart is read as 'heart attack,' dizziness as 'I will faint.' This fear raises arousal, which creates more symptoms — a vicious cycle.

points_json.example: Someone who hyperventilates during stress blows off too much carbon dioxide, causing tingling and dizziness — which they read as danger.
points_json.point: Biological factors include an oversensitive 'suffocation alarm' in the brain and low GABA activity. Genetics matter: panic disorder runs in families. Caffeine, alcohol withdrawal, and thyroid problems can trigger attacks.

points_json.example: A patient who stops driving on highways, then stops driving at all, then rarely leaves home.
points_json.point: Agoraphobic avoidance often grows with panic disorder. The person avoids places where escape feels hard or help unavailable. This avoidance shrinks life more than the attacks themselves and is the main target of treatment.

points_json.example: A patient practices spinning in a chair to create dizziness on purpose, learning that the feeling is harmless.
points_json.point: CBT for panic includes psychoeducation, breathing retraining, cognitive restructuring of catastrophic thoughts, and interoceptive exposure — deliberately creating feared sensations (spinning, fast breathing) to prove they are safe. This is the most effective treatment.

points_json.example: A patient on an SSRI finds her attacks drop from daily to monthly within 6 weeks.
points_json.point: Medicines that work: SSRIs and SNRIs are first-line. Benzodiazepines stop attacks fast but cause dependence and are only for short-term use. Combining CBT with medicine helps severe cases, but CBT alone has the best long-term results.

points_json.example: A recovered patient carries a card saying 'This is panic, not danger — it always passes in 10 minutes.'
points_json.point: Relapse prevention teaches that occasional symptoms are normal and not a sign of failure. Regular exercise, limited caffeine and alcohol, good sleep, and continued exposure practice keep recovery strong for years.

summary: Beyond the basics — the full picture of Panic Disorder: the 13 symptoms, why attacks spiral, agoraphobic avoidance, and the CBT techniques that stop them.
title: Panic Disorder in Depth

points_json.example: A mother who lies awake every night worrying about her children's safety, their grades, and family finances, even though nothing is actually wrong.
points_json.point: Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is excessive, hard-to-control worry about many everyday things — health, money, family, work — happening more days than not for at least 6 months. The worry feels impossible to switch off and the person knows it is excessive.

points_json.example: A GAD patient reports muscle tension so constant her shoulders ache daily, plus tiredness despite 8 hours in bed.
points_json.point: GAD needs 3 or more of these: restlessness, easy fatigue, trouble concentrating, irritability, muscle tension, and sleep problems. Children need only one. The symptoms must cause real distress or life problems.

points_json.example: A man who asks his wife ten times a day 'Are you sure the kids are okay?' and Googles every headache symptom for hours.
points_json.point: Worry behaviors maintain GAD: constant reassurance-seeking, over-preparing for unlikely disasters, procrastinating decisions, and avoiding uncertainty. These behaviors feel protective but actually feed the worry cycle.

points_json.example: A worrier who believes 'If I worry enough, I can prevent bad things' — and fears that relaxing means disaster will strike.
points_json.point: Metacognitive theory says GAD is driven by beliefs about worry itself: positive beliefs ('worrying keeps me safe') and negative beliefs ('worry will drive me crazy'). Treatment must challenge these beliefs, not just the worried thoughts.

points_json.example: Two sisters face the same job loss — the one with an anxious temperament develops GAD, the other does not.
points_json.point: Causes: genetics (GAD runs in families), an overactive amygdala and low GABA, childhood adversity, and a temperament high in neuroticism. Stressful life events often trigger the first episode in vulnerable people.

points_json.example: A patient learns to schedule a daily 20-minute 'worry time' — outside it, worries are postponed, not fought.
points_json.point: CBT for GAD includes worry awareness training, scheduled worry time, challenging the usefulness of worry, problem-solving training, and relaxation. Imaginal exposure to worst-case scenarios reduces their power.

points_json.example: A patient practices accepting uncertainty by deliberately taking small unplanned actions, like trying a new restaurant without reading reviews.
points_json.point: Intolerance of uncertainty is the core of GAD. Treatment builds tolerance through behavioral experiments — deliberately facing uncertain situations and discovering that discomfort passes and disasters rarely happen.

points_json.example: A GAD patient on an SNRI finds her constant tension eases within a month, letting therapy work better.
points_json.point: Medicines: SSRIs and SNRIs are first-line, buspirone is a non-addictive option, and pregabalin is used in some countries. CBT has more lasting effects than medicine alone — the best outcomes come from combining them.

summary: The worry that never switches off — GAD's diagnostic criteria, the worry cycle, intolerance of uncertainty, and the therapies that break it.
title: Generalized Anxiety Disorder in Depth

points_json.example: A university student who drops a required course because it involves a class presentation, delaying her graduation by a year.
points_json.point: Social Anxiety Disorder is intense fear of social situations where scrutiny is possible — speaking, eating in public, meeting strangers, using public toilets. The person fears acting in a way that brings humiliation or rejection. It must last 6 months or more.

points_json.example: A man who rehearses a 2-minute phone call for 30 minutes, then hangs up without dialing.
points_json.point: The cognitive model: socially anxious people hold a distorted mental image of how they appear, believe others judge harshly, and use safety behaviors (avoiding eye contact, rehearsing sentences, drinking to relax) that actually make interactions worse.

points_json.example: A teenager who was mocked for stuttering in class now fears all group situations.
points_json.point: Causes: genetics, an overactive fear circuit for social threats, childhood bullying or critical parenting, and embarrassing social experiences that condition the fear. It usually starts in early teens.

points_json.example: A woman who believes everyone at a party noticed her shaking hands — though nobody did.
points_json.point: Attention bias is central: socially anxious people focus inward on their symptoms and outward on signs of judgment, missing neutral or friendly cues. This creates a false sense of visible failure.

points_json.example: A patient deliberately asks a stranger for directions while maintaining eye contact, discovering the interaction goes fine.
points_json.point: CBT for social anxiety uses behavioral experiments, not just exposure — the patient tests predictions ('people will laugh') against reality. Dropping safety behaviors is key: no rehearsing, no hiding, no alcohol crutch.

points_json.example: A patient watches a video of her own speech and is shocked to see she looks calm — her feared image was completely wrong.
points_json.point: Video feedback corrects the distorted self-image. Patients predict they will look terrified, then see normal footage. This mismatch powerfully weakens the core belief of visible failure.

points_json.example: A student takes a beta-blocker before presentations to stop shaking, but still avoids all social events.
points_json.point: Medicines: SSRIs are first-line; beta-blockers help performance-only anxiety (shaky hands, racing heart) but not general social anxiety. Medicine plus CBT beats either alone for severe cases.

points_json.example: A recovered patient joins a debate club — the exact situation she once feared most.
points_json.point: Recovery means re-engaging with feared situations until they feel ordinary. Social skills training helps those who missed learning opportunities, and self-compassion replaces harsh self-criticism.

summary: The fear of being judged — how social anxiety distorts self-image, the safety behaviors that trap people, and the behavioral experiments that free them.
title: Social Anxiety Disorder in Depth

points_json.example: A student who takes a 2-hour bus route to avoid a 10-minute bridge crossing because of a fear of heights.
points_json.point: A Specific Phobia is marked fear of a particular object or situation — animals, heights, blood, flying, enclosed spaces, storms. The fear is out of proportion, lasts 6+ months, and leads to active avoidance. The person usually knows it is irrational.

points_json.example: A child bitten by a dog once develops a lifelong dog phobia.
points_json.point: DSM-5-TR lists four types: animal (dogs, spiders), natural environment (heights, water, storms), blood-injection-injury (needles, blood), and situational (flying, elevators, enclosed places). Blood phobia is unique — it causes fainting from a blood pressure drop, unlike other phobias.

points_json.example: A woman who faints at the sight of blood learns applied tension — tensing her muscles to keep blood pressure up.
points_json.point: Blood-injection-injury phobia has a two-phase response: heart rate first spikes, then drops sharply, causing fainting. Applied tension (tensing arm, chest, and leg muscles) prevents the faint and is the specific treatment.

points_json.example: A girl whose mother screamed at every spider grows up terrified of spiders without ever being bitten.
points_json.point: Causes: direct bad experiences (conditioning), watching others' fear (vicarious learning), scary stories and media (information transmission), and genetics. Evolution prepared us to fear snakes, spiders, and heights more easily.

points_json.example: A person afraid of flying watches crash news obsessively, which keeps the fear alive.
points_json.point: Avoidance maintains phobias: every avoided flight brings relief, which rewards the fear. Safety behaviors (always sitting near exits, carrying lucky charms) also prevent learning that the situation is safe.

points_json.example: A spider-phobic patient first looks at cartoon spiders, then photos, then a spider in a jar across the room — step by step.
points_json.point: Exposure therapy builds a fear hierarchy from least to most scary, then works up it gradually. The patient stays until anxiety drops. Virtual reality exposure now works well for flying and height phobias.

points_json.example: A flying-phobic patient takes one real flight with a therapist and is cured in a single 3-hour session.
points_json.point: Single-session exposure can cure many specific phobias in 2–3 hours — one of the fastest treatments in all of psychology. Flooding (immediate full exposure) works but is harder to tolerate than gradual steps.

points_json.example: A mother who calmly handles spiders teaches her children that spiders are harmless.
points_json.point: Prevention: calm parental modeling, accurate information about real risks, and early gentle exposure to feared things stop phobias before they form. Most childhood fears fade naturally and need no treatment.

summary: Irrational fears of specific things — the four phobia types, why blood phobia causes fainting, and the single-session cure that works in hours.
title: Specific Phobias in Depth

points_json.example: A woman who has not left her house alone in two years and only goes out when her brother walks with her.
points_json.point: Agoraphobia is fear of situations where escape might be difficult or help unavailable during panic-like symptoms: public transport, open spaces, enclosed places, crowds or lines, and being outside home alone. Two or more situations must be feared for 6+ months.

points_json.example: A man who can walk to the corner shop but panics at the shopping mall 2 km away.
points_json.point: The feared situations share one theme: being trapped without easy escape or rescue. Many sufferers can enter feared places with a trusted companion — the 'safe person' — but not alone. Distance from home often predicts fear intensity.

points_json.example: A patient who survived a panic attack on a bus now fears all buses, then trains, then any travel.
points_json.point: Agoraphobia often starts after panic attacks: the brain links the attack location with danger, then generalizes to similar places. But agoraphobia can also occur without any panic history — the fear is of incapacitation itself.

points_json.example: A sufferer who maps every public toilet, exit, and hospital on any new route.
points_json.point: Safety behaviors include always carrying water or medicine, sitting near exits, only going out at quiet times, and needing a mobile phone. These prevent the person from learning the feared catastrophe never happens.

points_json.example: A woman who quit her job, stopped visiting friends, and orders everything online.
points_json.point: The life cost is enormous: lost jobs, isolated relationships, and dependence on others. Agoraphobia has one of the highest disability levels among anxiety disorders because it restricts the entire geography of life.

points_json.example: A patient walks to the end of her street alone, waits until fear drops, then walks one block further the next day.
points_json.point: Treatment is graded in-vivo exposure: a hierarchy from easiest to hardest situations, practiced repeatedly until each feels safe. The companion is gradually faded out. This works even for decades-long agoraphobia.

points_json.example: A patient learns that a racing heart in a supermarket is uncomfortable but not dangerous — and stops fleeing.
points_json.point: CBT adds cognitive work: challenging beliefs like 'I will collapse and nobody will help.' Interoceptive exposure (creating feared body sensations) helps those whose agoraphobia is tied to panic symptoms.

points_json.example: An agoraphobic patient joins an online support group and discovers thousands share her exact experience.
points_json.point: Support matters: agoraphobia thrives in secrecy and shame. Support groups, family education (not over-accommodating avoidance), and SSRIs for severe cases all improve outcomes alongside exposure therapy.

summary: When the world shrinks to the size of home — the feared situations, the safe-person trap, and the graded exposure that rebuilds freedom step by step.
title: Agoraphobia in Depth

points_json.example: A student who loved cricket now feels empty, cannot get out of bed, has stopped eating, and cries daily for three weeks.
points_json.point: Major Depressive Disorder needs 5 or more of 9 symptoms for at least 2 weeks, and one must be depressed mood or anhedonia (loss of interest/pleasure). The 9 symptoms: low mood, no interest, weight/appetite change, sleep problems, restlessness or slowness, fatigue, worthlessness or guilt, poor concentration, and thoughts of death.

points_json.example: A man who smiles at work but goes home to sit in the dark for hours, feeling hollow inside.
points_json.point: Anhedonia — the inability to feel pleasure — is the most telling symptom. Smiling depression is real: many depressed people mask symptoms socially while suffering privately. Functioning at work does not rule out severe depression.

points_json.example: A woman whose depression is worst at 6 AM and lifts slightly by evening, who cannot enjoy even her grandchildren's visit.
points_json.point: Melancholic features: depression worst in mornings, complete loss of pleasure, early waking, major weight loss, and excessive guilt. This subtype responds better to medicines and ECT than to therapy alone.

points_json.example: A student who sleeps 12 hours, gains weight, and feels briefly better when friends visit — then crashes again.
points_json.point: Atypical features are the reverse: mood lifts with positive events, but with heavy leaden limbs, sleeping too much, eating too much, and extreme sensitivity to rejection. It is common and often missed.

points_json.example: A new mother who cries all day, feels she is a bad mother, and cannot bond with her baby.
points_json.point: Peripartum onset means depression during pregnancy or within 4 weeks after birth (clinically, up to a year). It affects about 1 in 7 mothers. It is a medical condition, not weakness — and it is highly treatable.

points_json.example: A depressed man who hears a voice saying he is evil and deserves punishment.
points_json.point: With psychotic features, depression includes delusions (often guilt-themed) or hallucinations. This is severe and needs urgent treatment — usually antidepressants plus antipsychotics, or ECT.

points_json.example: A patient who failed twice on SSRIs finally recovers with a different class of medicine plus CBT.
points_json.point: Treatment-resistant depression means failing 2+ adequate medicine trials. Options: switching medicine classes, adding therapy, ECT (most effective for severe cases), TMS (magnetic brain stimulation), esketamine nasal spray, and newer options.

points_json.example: A recovered patient notices sleep worsening and calls her therapist early — catching relapse before it blooms.
points_json.point: Depression is recurrent: half of patients relapse. Maintenance treatment (continuing medicine or therapy), mindfulness-based cognitive therapy, regular exercise, and early warning plans cut relapse rates dramatically.

summary: Depression's many faces — the 9 criteria, melancholic vs atypical subtypes, psychotic depression, peripartum depression, and what works when nothing works.
title: Major Depressive Disorder in Depth

points_json.example: A man who has felt low, tired, and hopeless almost every day for 3 years, yet still goes to work — he thinks this is just his personality.
points_json.point: Persistent Depressive Disorder (dysthymia) is depressed mood more days than not for at least 2 years (1 year in children), plus 2+ milder symptoms: poor appetite or overeating, sleep problems, low energy, low self-esteem, poor concentration, hopelessness. The person functions, but life always feels grey.

points_json.example: A woman who has had dysthymia for years, then sinks into a full major depressive episode on top of it.
points_json.point: Double depression means major depressive episodes striking on top of chronic dysthymia. It is common and harder to treat than either alone — but treating the major episode first often lifts the baseline too.

points_json.example: A teenager who has been irritable and gloomy since age 12, and cannot remember ever feeling truly happy.
points_json.point: Early-onset dysthymia (before 21) often goes unrecognized for years because the person — and family — mistake it for personality. 'She's always been moody' delays treatment by a decade on average.

points_json.example: A dysthymic patient who cancels plans weekly because 'what's the point, I won't enjoy it anyway.'
points_json.point: The quiet damage: dysthymia erodes relationships, careers, and health slowly. People stop trying, assume unhappiness is normal, and never seek help. It raises the risk of full major depression, anxiety, and substance use.

points_json.example: A patient who believed she was 'just a negative person' weeps with relief learning her condition has a name and treatment.
points_json.point: Causes: genetics, chronic stress, childhood adversity, low serotonin function, and thinking styles (rumination, pessimism). Dysthymia is not a character flaw — it is a recognized medical disorder.

points_json.example: A dysthymic patient starts CBASP therapy, learning to connect her actions with real outcomes in relationships.
points_json.point: CBASP (Cognitive Behavioral Analysis System of Psychotherapy) was designed for chronic depression: it focuses on interpersonal cause-and-effect, helping patients see that their behavior does influence how others respond.

points_json.example: A patient on long-term SSRI treatment finds her baseline mood lifts from 'grey' to 'okay' over 3 months.
points_json.point: Medicines work for dysthymia but take longer — 8 to 12 weeks for full effect. Because the condition is chronic, treatment is usually long-term. Combining medicine with therapy gives the best results.

points_json.example: A recovered patient keeps a mood diary and notices winters are hardest — planning extra light exposure and activity.
points_json.point: Management is marathon, not sprint: ongoing therapy check-ins, behavioral activation (scheduling pleasant activities even without motivation), exercise, sleep regularity, and treating co-occurring anxiety all protect the gains.

summary: The depression that never quite leaves — chronic low mood mistaken for personality, double depression, and the long-term treatments that lift the grey.
title: Dysthymia and Chronic Depression

points_json.example: A man who slept 2 hours a night for a week, spent his family's savings on 3 cars, and believes he is about to become a famous inventor.
points_json.point: Bipolar I Disorder requires at least one manic episode: a distinct week (or any length if hospitalized) of abnormally elevated or irritable mood plus 3+ symptoms — grandiosity, less sleep need, talkativeness, racing thoughts, distractibility, increased activity, risky behavior. Psychosis may occur.

points_json.example: A manic patient who believes he is a prophet and hears God commanding him to preach in the streets.
points_json.point: Psychotic features in mania are usually mood-congruent: grandiose delusions (special powers, divine mission) and hallucinations matching the elevated mood. These signal severe mania needing urgent treatment, often hospitalization.

points_json.example: A woman who maxed out 5 credit cards, had affairs, and quit her job during a 3-week manic episode she cannot fully remember.
points_json.point: The wreckage of mania: ruined finances, broken relationships, lost jobs, legal trouble, and sexually transmitted infections. The shame afterward often triggers a crushing depressive crash — the cycle's cruelest turn.

points_json.example: A patient who misses the energy and confidence of mania and secretly stops her medicine to feel 'alive' again.
points_json.point: Poor insight is common: many patients enjoy mania and stop treatment. This is the top cause of relapse. Psychoeducation helps patients recognize mania as illness, not their 'true self,' and spot early warning signs.

points_json.example: A bipolar patient whose mother and uncle both had the disorder — and whose episodes began at 19.
points_json.point: Bipolar I is among the most heritable mental disorders (60–80%). It usually starts in late teens to twenties. Stressful events, sleep loss, and antidepressants without mood stabilizers can trigger first episodes.

points_json.example: A manic patient calmed within days on an antipsychotic, then stabilized long-term on lithium.
points_json.point: Acute mania treatment: second-generation antipsychotics work fastest; lithium and valproate are classic mood stabilizers. Severe mania with psychosis may need hospitalization. Never use antidepressants alone — they can flip mania worse.

points_json.example: A stable patient on lithium gets blood tests every 3 months and has been episode-free for 4 years.
points_json.point: Maintenance is lifelong for most: lithium remains the gold standard (it also reduces suicide risk), with valproate, lamotrigine, or atypical antipsychotics as alternatives. Stopping medicine causes relapse in most patients within a year.

points_json.example: A patient and family create a crisis plan: warning signs, who to call, which hospital, medication list.
points_json.point: Beyond pills: regular sleep (the top protective factor), Interpersonal and Social Rhythm Therapy, family-focused therapy, and advance crisis plans. With treatment, most people with Bipolar I live full, stable lives.

summary: The highs that destroy and the crashes that follow — manic episodes, psychotic mania, why patients stop medicine, and the lifelong treatment that stabilizes.
title: Bipolar I Disorder in Depth

points_json.example: A woman who for 4 days feels unusually cheerful, needs only 4 hours of sleep, and starts 5 new projects — but still goes to work and functions.
points_json.point: Bipolar II Disorder needs at least one hypomanic episode (4+ days of elevated mood and energy, noticeable to others, without severe damage or psychosis) plus at least one major depressive episode. Hypomania alone is never enough — the depression is required.

points_json.example: A Bipolar II patient whose depressions last 6 months each, with 3 suicide attempts — while her hypomanias last only days.
points_json.point: Bipolar II is NOT milder than Bipolar I overall. The hypomanias are gentler, but the depressions are often longer, deeper, and carry higher suicide risk. Patients spend far more time depressed than high.

points_json.example: A patient treated for 'depression' with antidepressants alone flips into agitation and impulsivity.
points_json.point: The great misdiagnosis: Bipolar II is often mistaken for major depression because patients seek help during depression, not hypomania (which feels good). Antidepressants alone can trigger hypomania or rapid cycling — always screen for past highs.

points_json.example: A doctor asks: 'Have you ever had a period of needing much less sleep yet feeling full of energy?' — and the patient remembers.
points_json.point: Key screening questions: periods of unusually high energy, racing thoughts, risky spending or behavior, and others commenting on the change. Collateral from family is gold — patients forget or minimize hypomanic episodes.

points_json.example: A student who for 2 years swings between mildly high-energy weeks and mildly low weeks, never fully stable, never fully ill.
points_json.point: Cyclothymic Disorder is chronic mild swinging: 2+ years (1 year in youth) of hypomanic-like and depressive-like symptoms that never meet full criteria, with no symptom-free gap longer than 2 months. It causes real life problems despite being 'mild.'

points_json.example: A cyclothymic teenager whose mood swings are dismissed as 'just being a teenager' for years.
points_json.point: Cyclothymia often starts in teens and is mistaken for personality. About one-third of cases progress to Bipolar I or II. Early treatment with mood stabilizers and rhythm therapy can prevent this progression.

points_json.example: A Bipolar II patient stabilized on lamotrigine plus therapy, with a strict sleep schedule.
points_json.point: Treatment: mood stabilizers (lamotrigine is favored for Bipolar II depression, lithium and valproate also used), cautious antidepressant use only with a stabilizer, and psychotherapy focused on sleep regularity and early warning detection.

points_json.example: A patient tracks mood daily on an app and spots her hypomania by day 2 — calling her doctor before damage is done.
points_json.point: Mood charting is powerful: daily tracking of sleep, mood, and medicine reveals patterns and catches episodes early. Family involvement in monitoring doubles the chance of early intervention.

summary: The quieter highs and deeper lows — why Bipolar II is often misdiagnosed as depression, the hidden dangers of hypomania, and cyclothymia's chronic swing.
title: Bipolar II and Cyclothymia

points_json.example: A 22-year-old university student who was doing well suddenly insists the TV is sending him secret messages and stops attending classes.
points_json.point: Schizophrenia needs 2+ of 5 key symptoms for 6 months: delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized/catatonic behavior, and negative symptoms. One must be delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized speech. Functioning must clearly decline.

points_json.example: A patient hears two voices commenting on everything she does, and believes her neighbors planted cameras in her walls.
points_json.point: Positive symptoms add abnormal experiences: persecutory delusions (being spied on), grandiose or bizarre delusions, auditory hallucinations (voices commenting or commanding), disorganized speech (jumping topics, invented words), and odd behavior.

points_json.example: A man who sits silently all day, shows no expression when his sister visits, and has stopped showering.
points_json.point: Negative symptoms take things away: flat affect (no emotional expression), alogia (very little speech), avolition (no motivation), anhedonia (no pleasure), and asociality. These predict long-term disability more than hallucinations do.

points_json.example: A patient who cannot follow a 3-step recipe she once knew, or hold a simple cashier job.
points_json.point: Cognitive symptoms — poor attention, weak working memory, trouble planning — are now seen as core to schizophrenia. They exist before psychosis appears and best predict whether someone can work or study.

points_json.example: A young man whose grades slipped for a year, who withdrew from friends and acted oddly — months before any voices appeared.
points_json.point: The prodrome: most patients show a gradual decline — social withdrawal, odd beliefs, falling school or work performance — for months or years before the first psychotic break. Early intervention during this phase improves outcomes greatly.

points_json.example: Drugs like cocaine that raise dopamine can trigger temporary psychosis — supporting the dopamine link.
points_json.point: The dopamine hypothesis: overactive dopamine in the mesolimbic pathway drives hallucinations and delusions. Brain scans show enlarged ventricles and thinner frontal cortex. Genetics are strong — identical twin risk is about 50%.

points_json.example: A patient stable for a year stops his tablets feeling cured — within weeks the voices return.
points_json.point: Antipsychotics are the foundation: they block dopamine and control positive symptoms. Newer (atypical) drugs are preferred. Stopping medicine is the top cause of relapse — long-acting injections help those who struggle with daily pills.

points_json.example: A recovered patient works part-time with a job coach while attending a weekly social skills group.
points_json.point: Recovery needs more than pills: CBT for psychosis challenges distressing beliefs, family therapy cuts relapse, supported employment rebuilds work life, and cognitive remediation trains memory and attention. Many patients recover meaningful lives.

summary: Reality breaking down — the full diagnostic picture, the warning prodrome, why negative symptoms disable most, and the combination of treatments that rebuilds lives.
title: Schizophrenia in Depth

points_json.example: A woman who functions perfectly at work but is convinced her boss is secretly in love with her despite zero evidence.
points_json.point: Delusional Disorder means holding at least one strong delusion for a month or more, while otherwise thinking and behavior look normal. Unlike schizophrenia, hallucinations are absent or minor, and daily functioning is often preserved outside the delusion's topic.

points_json.example: A man who believes his coworkers poison his lunch daily, yet chats normally about football and does his job well.
points_json.point: The delusions are non-bizarre — things that could happen in real life (being followed, poisoned, loved, cheated on). This is why the disorder hides so well: the person seems rational about everything except the one fixed belief.

points_json.example: A jealous husband who checks his wife's phone nightly, convinced of affairs with no proof, for 3 years.
points_json.point: DSM-5-TR types: persecutory (most common — being conspired against), jealous (partner unfaithful), grandiose (special powers or identity), erotomanic (someone famous in love with them), somatic (body infested or diseased), and mixed.

points_json.example: An erotomanic patient who sends 50 letters to a news anchor, convinced their 'secret love' is real.
points_json.point: Erotomanic delusions can lead to stalking behavior and legal trouble. Jealous delusions carry risk of violence toward the partner. Persecutory delusions may prompt complaints to police or courts — all while the person seems otherwise sane.

points_json.example: A patient whose delusion began after he started mishearing conversations due to hearing loss.
points_json.point: Risk factors: older age, social isolation, sensory impairment (hearing or vision loss), immigration stress, and family history of psychosis. Isolation lets the delusion grow unchallenged — a key reason it persists.

points_json.example: A lonely widower whose persecutory beliefs softened after joining a daily community group.
points_json.point: Why it persists: the delusion explains confusing experiences, protects self-esteem, and goes unchallenged in isolation. Confronting it directly backfires — the person digs in deeper.

points_json.example: A therapist who never argues about the delusion but helps the patient sleep better and rejoin activities.
points_json.point: Treatment approach: build trust first, never directly challenge the belief. Treat co-occurring depression or anxiety, improve sleep and social contact, and use antipsychotics cautiously — response is modest compared to schizophrenia.

points_json.example: A patient who still believes the delusion but has returned to work and stopped harassing the 'persecutors.'
points_json.point: Realistic goals: full insight is rare. Success means reduced distress, better functioning, and less harmful behavior — even if the core belief remains. Long-term supportive contact prevents deterioration.

summary: One fixed false belief in an otherwise rational mind — the six delusion types, why confrontation fails, and the gentle treatment that actually helps.
title: Delusional Disorder in Depth

points_json.example: A man who develops delusions and hallucinations for 3 weeks after his brother's sudden death, then fully recovers.
points_json.point: Brief Psychotic Disorder is sudden psychosis — delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized speech — lasting at least 1 day but less than 1 month, with full return to normal. It often follows extreme stress like bereavement or trauma.

points_json.example: A new mother who within a week of delivery believes her baby is possessed and hears commanding voices.
points_json.point: Postpartum onset is a classic trigger: brief psychosis can erupt within weeks of childbirth. This is a psychiatric emergency — the risk to mother and baby is high, and urgent hospitalization is usually needed.

points_json.example: A student who after 10 days of symptoms is already back in class, puzzled by what happened.
points_json.point: Good prognostic signs: sudden onset, short duration, severe stressor as trigger, no family history of schizophrenia, and good prior functioning. Most people recover completely and never relapse.

points_json.example: A patient whose 'brief' episode stretches past a month becomes a different diagnosis.
points_json.point: The one-month line matters: if symptoms last 1–6 months, the diagnosis becomes schizophreniform disorder. Past 6 months with decline, it becomes schizophrenia. Accurate timeline tracking changes everything.

points_json.example: A traveler who after 3 sleepless nights and culture shock develops paranoid beliefs that resolve with rest.
points_json.point: Not all brief psychosis is primary: severe sleep deprivation, drugs (cannabis, stimulants), and medical causes (infections, thyroid storm) can mimic it. Ruling these out is the first clinical step.

points_json.example: A patient calmed within days on a short course of antipsychotics, then tapered off completely.
points_json.point: Treatment: brief antipsychotic courses, treating the trigger (grief counseling, sleep restoration), and safety monitoring. Unlike schizophrenia, long-term medicine is usually unnecessary — a hopeful difference.

points_json.example: A woman who had one brief episode after assault, then stayed well for 10 years with therapy support.
points_json.point: Follow-up is still wise: a minority later develop schizophrenia or bipolar disorder. One year of monitoring, stress management skills, and family education protect against recurrence.

points_json.example: A family taught to watch for warning signs — sleeplessness, odd beliefs — and call early rather than waiting.
points_json.point: Prevention of recurrence: sleep protection (the top trigger), stress management, avoiding drugs, and an early-warning plan with the family. Most people with brief psychotic disorder live normal lives afterward.

summary: Psychosis that arrives suddenly and leaves completely — triggers, the critical one-month boundary, postpartum emergencies, and why prognosis is hopeful.
title: Brief Psychotic Disorder

points_json.example: A woman who idealizes her new friend as perfect on Monday, then hates her as cruel on Wednesday because she replied late to a message.
points_json.point: Borderline Personality Disorder means instability in relationships, self-image, and emotions, plus impulsivity. DSM-5-TR needs 5 of 9 features: frantic abandonment fears, unstable intense relationships, identity disturbance, impulsivity, self-harm, emotional instability, emptiness, intense anger, and stress-related paranoia.

points_json.example: A patient who cuts her arms when her therapist goes on holiday, terrified of being abandoned.
points_json.point: Frantic efforts to avoid abandonment — real or imagined — drive much BPD behavior: desperate texts, threats, self-harm. The pain of perceived rejection is experienced as unbearable, not dramatic.

points_json.example: A man who describes himself as 'a chameleon — I become whoever I'm with because I don't know who I am.'
points_json.point: Identity disturbance: a shifting, unstable self-image — changing goals, values, friend groups, even sexuality. Chronic emptiness sits underneath: a hollow feeling patients describe as painful numbness.

points_json.example: A patient who rages at a cashier over small change, then sobs with shame an hour later.
points_json.point: Emotional dysregulation is the core: emotions spike fast, peak intensely, and fade slowly. Anger is especially prominent. This is now seen as a brain-based sensitivity, not manipulation.

points_json.example: A teenager whose repeated self-cutting finally brings her to a DBT program.
points_json.point: Self-harm and suicidality are common — about 10% die by suicide. Self-harm usually regulates unbearable emotion, not seeks attention. Every threat must be taken seriously and risk-assessed.

points_json.example: A BPD patient who was sexually abused as a child and grew up with an emotionally dismissive mother.
points_json.point: Causes: the biosocial model — an emotionally sensitive child plus an invalidating environment (abuse, neglect, or simply dismissed feelings). Genetics contribute about 40–60%. It is nobody's fault.

points_json.example: A patient in DBT learns to hold ice cubes instead of cutting when pain feels unbearable.
points_json.point: DBT (Dialectical Behavior Therapy) is the gold standard: mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, and interpersonal effectiveness skills. It strongly reduces self-harm and hospitalizations. MBT (mentalization-based therapy) also works well.

points_json.example: A recovered patient who once attempted suicide now holds a steady job and a stable marriage after 3 years of DBT.
points_json.point: Prognosis is better than believed: most patients improve substantially within 5–10 years. Medicines treat co-occurring depression or anxiety, not BPD itself. Long-term therapy and stable relationships heal.

summary: The disorder of unstable everything — the 9 features, why abandonment terror drives self-harm, the biosocial causes, and DBT's life-saving skills.
title: Borderline Personality Disorder in Depth

points_json.example: A man who scams elderly people out of savings, gets arrested, and blames the victims for being foolish.
points_json.point: Antisocial Personality Disorder means a persistent pattern of disregarding others' rights since age 15: deceitfulness, impulsivity, aggression, irresponsibility, and lack of remorse. Diagnosis only at 18+, with conduct disorder before 15.

points_json.example: A teenager who tortures animals, sets fires, and steals cars — the childhood warning signs.
points_json.point: Conduct disorder before 15 is required: aggression to people or animals, property destruction, theft, serious rule-breaking. Childhood-onset conduct disorder predicts worse adult outcomes than adolescent-onset.

points_json.example: A con artist who cries convincingly to gain trust, then empties the victim's bank account without a flicker of guilt.
points_json.point: Superficial charm and manipulation are hallmarks. Many are skilled liars who mimic emotions without feeling them. Lack of remorse is defining — harm to others brings indifference or rationalization, never genuine guilt.

points_json.example: A corporate executive who commits fraud, ruins colleagues' careers, and feels entitled to it all.
points_json.point: The 'successful psychopath': ASPD exists on a spectrum. Some end up in prisons; others in boardrooms, using the same traits — charm, ruthlessness, fearlessness — in white-collar settings.

points_json.example: Brain scans show reduced amygdala response to others' fear — the neural basis of missing empathy.
points_json.point: Causes: strong genetics, low arousal (seeking stimulation through risk), childhood abuse and neglect, inconsistent parenting, and peer delinquency. Fearlessness in childhood predicts later antisocial behavior.

points_json.example: A young offender in multisystemic therapy whose family, school, and peers are all engaged — and whose offending drops.
points_json.point: Treatment is difficult but not hopeless: structured programs work best in youth (multisystemic therapy, parent training). Adults respond poorly to insight therapy; contingency-based programs with clear rewards and consequences work better.

points_json.example: A prison program that rewards prosocial behavior with privileges sees reoffending drop.
points_json.point: In forensic settings, token economies and cognitive-behavioral programs targeting criminal thinking reduce reoffending. Punishment alone does not rehabilitate — skills training does.

points_json.example: A former offender who at 45 has 'burned out' — the impulsivity faded with age, and he now mentors at-risk youth.
points_json.point: Prognosis: ASPD often mellows with age — the 'burnout' phenomenon by middle age. Stable relationships, employment, and aging all reduce symptoms. Early intervention in conduct-disordered youth is the best prevention.

summary: Charm without conscience — the conduct disorder roots, the empathy gap in the brain, why therapy often fails, and what actually reduces reoffending.
title: Antisocial Personality Disorder in Depth

points_json.example: A boss who takes credit for all team work, calls struggling employees weak, and flies into rage at mild criticism.
points_json.point: Narcissistic Personality Disorder means grandiosity, constant need for admiration, and lack of empathy — 5 of 9 features: grandiose self-importance, fantasies of unlimited success, belief in being special, excessive admiration needs, entitlement, exploitative behavior, no empathy, envy, and arrogance.

points_json.example: A man who name-drops celebrities, exaggerates achievements, and expects the best table without booking.
points_json.point: Two faces: grandiose narcissism (overt arrogance, dominance) and vulnerable narcissism (hypersensitive, shy, but equally entitled and resentful). Both share fragile self-esteem hidden under the surface.

points_json.example: A narcissistic father who loves his child as an extension of himself — proud when the child wins, cold when the child fails.
points_json.point: Relationships suffer most: partners feel used, children feel conditional love. The narcissist idealizes then devalues — intense admiration flipping to contempt when admiration stops.

points_json.example: A woman raised by a narcissistic mother who was praised only for achievements, never for just existing.
points_json.point: Causes: excessive pampering or excessive criticism in childhood, both teaching that love is conditional on being special. Genetics contribute. Culture matters — individualistic societies show rising narcissism scores.

points_json.example: A narcissist who crumbles into depression when his business fails — the grandiosity was protecting deep shame.
points_json.point: Underneath is fragile self-esteem: criticism triggers narcissistic injury — rage or collapse. This vulnerability is why many narcissists also develop depression when reality punctures the fantasy.

points_json.example: A patient who storms out of therapy when the therapist gently notes a mistake.
points_json.point: Therapy challenges: narcissists rarely seek help (others have the problem), devalue therapists, and quit when challenged. Successful therapy requires the therapist to survive devaluation without retaliating.

points_json.example: A therapist who acknowledges the patient's real strengths while slowly building empathy exercises.
points_json.point: What helps: schema therapy and transference-focused therapy show promise — building genuine self-worth to replace grandiosity, and practicing perspective-taking. Progress is slow but real.

points_json.example: A former patient who learns to ask his wife about her day — and actually listen.
points_json.point: Prognosis: change is possible, especially with age and life consequences. Building real accomplishments, stable relationships, and self-compassion gradually replaces the need for constant admiration.

summary: Grandiosity hiding fragility — the 9 features, grandiose vs vulnerable types, the devaluation cycle in relationships, and therapies that build real self-worth.
title: Narcissistic Personality Disorder in Depth

points_json.example: A manager who rewrites every team report himself because nobody meets his impossible standards, then misses every deadline.
points_json.point: Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder means extreme preoccupation with order, perfectionism, and control — 4 of 8 features: details over the big picture, perfectionism that blocks completion, workaholism, over-conscientiousness, hoarding worthless things, reluctance to delegate, miserliness, and rigidity.

points_json.example: A student who rewrites the same essay introduction 30 times and submits nothing.
points_json.point: Perfectionism that paralyzes: the need for flawlessness prevents finishing anything. This differs from healthy high standards — here the standards are impossible and the cost is everything else in life.

points_json.example: A father who schedules family fun in 15-minute blocks and explodes when plans change.
points_json.point: Rigidity rules life: moral inflexibility, inability to discard worn-out objects, stinginess with money and emotions, and relationships sacrificed to work. Others experience the person as controlling, not caring.

points_json.example: A common confusion: OCPD has NO true obsessions or compulsions — unlike OCD, where unwanted intrusive thoughts drive rituals.
points_json.point: OCPD vs OCD: OCPD traits feel right to the person (ego-syntonic) — 'my way is correct.' OCD rituals feel wrong and unwanted (ego-dystonic). They can co-occur but are different disorders needing different approaches.

points_json.example: A child raised by harsh, punishing parents who learned that mistakes bring harsh consequences.
points_json.point: Causes: genetics, anxious temperament, and overly strict or critical parenting that teaches love must be earned through flawlessness. Culture's work ethic can reinforce it.

points_json.example: A workaholic who has not taken a holiday in 8 years and whose marriage is collapsing.
points_json.point: The hidden suffering: underneath control is anxiety — fear that relaxing standards means disaster. Depression and burnout are common when the impossible standards inevitably fail.

points_json.example: A patient who practices deliberately sending an email with one small typo — and surviving.
points_json.point: Treatment: CBT challenges all-or-nothing thinking and perfectionist rules; behavioral experiments test 'good enough.' Relaxation and scheduled leisure rebuild a life beyond work. Insight comes slowly — the traits feel like virtues.

points_json.example: A recovered manager who now delegates, takes weekends off, and laughs at small mistakes.
points_json.point: Prognosis is good with therapy: learning flexibility, accepting imperfection, and reconnecting with relationships. Many channel the conscientiousness positively once rigidity softens.

summary: Perfectionism as a prison — how OCPD differs from OCD, the 8 features, why control masks anxiety, and the experiments that teach 'good enough.'
title: Obsessive-Compulsive PD in Depth

points_json.example: A contamination-OCD patient touches a public railing and waits without washing. After 30 minutes the anxiety fades on its own.
points_json.point: ERP (Exposure and Response Prevention) is the gold-standard OCD treatment. The patient faces the feared trigger (exposure) while resisting the compulsion (response prevention). Anxiety spikes, then naturally falls — teaching the brain the fear was false. About 70% improve significantly.

points_json.example: A checking-OCD patient's hierarchy: look at a locked door photo (20/100 fear), lock once and walk away for 1 minute (50/100), leave home after one check (90/100).
points_json.point: Step 1 is building a fear hierarchy: ranking triggers from least to most distressing (0–100 scale). Treatment starts low and climbs gradually. Each step is repeated until distress drops by half before moving up.

points_json.example: A patient who usually taps the doorway 4 times walks through without tapping — hands shaking, but walking.
points_json.point: Step 2 is response prevention: the hard part. The patient agrees in advance which compulsions to drop. The therapist coaches through the urge without giving reassurance — because reassurance is itself a compulsion.

points_json.example: A patient records a loop tape saying 'the house will burn down because you didn't check' and listens until it feels boring.
points_json.point: Imaginal exposure handles fears that can't be staged live — like causing a disaster. The patient vividly imagines the worst outcome repeatedly until the horror fades. This tackles the obsession, not just the ritual.

points_json.example: A therapist who refuses to answer 'Are you sure my hands are clean?' — kindly, every time.
points_json.point: Family accommodation must stop: answering reassurance questions, doing rituals for the patient, or changing routines around OCD. Families learn supportive non-participation — love without feeding the disorder.

points_json.example: A patient on a high-dose SSRI finds her intrusive thoughts quieter, making ERP exercises possible.
points_json.point: SSRIs at higher doses than for depression boost ERP success, especially for severe OCD. Combined treatment beats either alone. For treatment-resistant cases, adding a low-dose antipsychotic or trying deep TMS are options.

points_json.example: A patient who completed ERP but starts avoiding again is told: 'Lapses are data, not failure — restart exposure this week.'
points_json.point: Relapse prevention: OCD is chronic for many, so booster sessions matter. Patients keep an exposure practice schedule, monitor early warning signs, and re-enter treatment quickly at the first slip.

points_json.example: A teenager whose OCD centered on religious blasphemy thoughts learns they are just brain noise, not moral truth.
points_json.point: ERP works for all OCD themes — contamination, harm, religious, sexual, symmetry. The content of obsessions doesn't change the method: face the trigger, drop the ritual, let anxiety habituate. Shame about taboo themes needs direct, normalizing discussion.

summary: The therapy that beats OCD — how ERP hierarchies are built, why response prevention is the hard part, family accommodation, and relapse prevention.
title: OCD: Treatment Focus (ERP in Detail)

points_json.example: A student who pulls out her eyebrows during exam stress until they are completely gone.
points_json.point: Trichotillomania (hair-pulling disorder) means repeatedly pulling out hair — scalp, eyebrows, eyelashes — causing visible loss. The person has tried to stop but the urge feels irresistible, especially during stress, boredom, or while half-focused (reading, watching TV).

points_json.example: A woman who picks at her skin for an hour each night, creating sores she then hides with makeup.
points_json.point: Excoriation (skin-picking disorder) is the parallel condition: repeatedly picking skin, causing wounds and scarring. Both disorders bring shame and secrecy — many sufferers hide the behavior for years before seeking help.

points_json.example: A puller who describes a 'tingling itch' on the scalp that only pulling relieves — then guilt immediately after.
points_json.point: The behavior cycle: rising tension or urge, the pulling/picking (often trance-like), then relief mixed with shame. Two styles exist — focused (deliberate, urge-driven) and automatic (unconscious, during other activities).

points_json.example: A teenager who started pulling after her parents' divorce, when anxiety felt unmanageable.
points_json.point: Causes: genetics, problems with impulse control circuits in the brain, and emotional triggers — anxiety, boredom, frustration. It is NOT self-harm: the goal is tension relief, not pain or injury.

points_json.example: A patient who wears gloves while studying and keeps a fidget toy in her pocket — pulling drops by half in 2 weeks.
points_json.point: Habit Reversal Training (HRT) is the core treatment: awareness training (noticing urges), competing responses (clenching fists, holding objects), and stimulus control (gloves, bandages, changing routines). It works well for both disorders.

points_json.example: A skin-picker who replaces evening picking with a 20-minute walk plus moisturizer routine.
points_json.point: Stimulus control redesigns the environment: keeping hands busy, removing tweezers and mirrors, dimming bathroom lights, covering target areas. Small environmental changes produce large behavior drops.

points_json.example: A patient on N-acetylcysteine (a supplement) finds her pulling urges weaken noticeably.
points_json.point: Medicines: N-acetylcysteine shows promise for both disorders; SSRIs help when anxiety or OCD co-occur. Treating the underlying anxiety or boredom matters as much as targeting the habit itself.

points_json.example: A recovered patient who still gets urges during finals but rides them out with her competing-response skills.
points_json.point: These are chronic, waxing-waning conditions — stress brings flare-ups. Long-term management means keeping HRT skills sharp, maintaining support, and treating urges as signals to address stress, not as failures.

summary: The hidden hair-pulling and skin-picking disorders — the urge cycle, why it's not self-harm, Habit Reversal Training, and long-term management.
title: Trichotillomania and Excoriation in Depth

points_json.example: In prolonged exposure, a survivor describes the assault in detail session after session — by week 8, telling the story no longer causes panic.
points_json.point: Prolonged Exposure (PE) revisits the trauma memory and avoided situations until they lose power. Sessions include imaginal recounting of the trauma and in-vivo exposure to safe-but-avoided triggers. It is one of the two most evidence-backed PTSD treatments.

points_json.example: A veteran who avoided fireworks for years watches a display with his therapist — and stays.
points_json.point: How PE works: avoidance maintains PTSD by preventing new learning. Repeated safe exposure teaches the brain that memories and reminders are not dangerous now. Homework between sessions is essential — therapy alone is not enough.

points_json.example: A patient follows the therapist's fingers with her eyes while recalling the crash — and the memory's sting fades.
points_json.point: EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing) pairs trauma recall with bilateral stimulation (eye movements, taps). The patient processes the memory until it feels distant. It works as well as PE, often in fewer sessions.

points_json.example: A survivor who believed 'the attack was my fault for walking alone' learns to examine the evidence fairly.
points_json.point: Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT) targets trauma's stuck beliefs — self-blame, distrust, helplessness. Patients write about the trauma's meaning and systematically challenge distorted thoughts over about 12 sessions.

points_json.example: A patient on an SSRI finds nightmares fade and therapy becomes possible.
points_json.point: Medicines: SSRIs and SNRIs are first-line for PTSD; prazosin specifically reduces trauma nightmares. Medicine plus trauma-focused therapy beats either alone for severe cases.

points_json.example: A survivor who was forced to recount trauma before she felt safe got worse — and needed months to trust therapy again.
points_json.point: What NOT to do: never force disclosure before safety and trust are built. Debriefing everyone right after disasters can harm. Treatment must be paced — stabilization first, trauma processing second.

points_json.example: A group of veterans who share stories and realize 'I'm not the only one' — healing through belonging.
points_json.point: Group therapy, family involvement, and peer support amplify recovery. PTSD isolates; connection heals. Treating co-occurring depression, substance use, and sleep problems is part of complete care.

points_json.example: A recovered survivor who still startles at loud bangs but lives fully — working, loving, sleeping well.
points_json.point: Recovery is realistic: most patients improve substantially with trauma-focused therapy. Some symptoms may linger mildly, but the disorder no longer runs life. Post-traumatic growth — deeper meaning and strength — is common.

summary: How PTSD is actually treated — Prolonged Exposure, EMDR, and Cognitive Processing Therapy explained step by step, plus what to avoid.
title: PTSD Treatment Approaches

points_json.example: A 7-year-old who flinches when adults raise their hands, though nobody in her current home has ever hit her.
points_json.point: Childhood trauma — abuse, neglect, witnessing violence — shapes the developing brain. The stress system gets stuck on high alert: traumatized children may be hypervigilant, aggressive, or dissociated, often misdiagnosed with ADHD or bipolar disorder.

points_json.example: Brain scans show smaller hippocampus and overactive amygdala in adults abused as children.
points_json.point: The biology: chronic childhood stress floods the brain with cortisol during critical growth periods. This shrinks memory centers, sensitizes fear circuits, and weakens the prefrontal cortex's calming control — effects visible decades later.

points_json.example: A neglected toddler who rocks alone for hours and does not seek comfort when hurt.
points_json.point: Attachment damage: abuse and neglect disrupt the safe bond children need. Reactive attachment disorder (withdrawn, unresponsive) and disinhibited social engagement (overfriendly with strangers) are the two diagnosed outcomes of severe neglect.

points_json.example: A 12-year-old who alternates between rage, numbness, and panic — diagnosed with 4 different disorders by different doctors.
points_json.point: Developmental Trauma Disorder (proposed, not yet in DSM) captures what complex childhood trauma creates: emotional dysregulation, attention problems, and relationship difficulties together. Standard PTSD criteria often miss this childhood picture.

points_json.example: An adult who was beaten as a child and now beats his own children — until therapy breaks the cycle.
points_json.point: Intergenerational transmission is real but not destiny: about one-third of abused children become abusive parents. Awareness, therapy, and support break the cycle — most survivors do NOT repeat the abuse.

points_json.example: A foster child who thrives after placement with a patient, predictable caregiver.
points_json.point: What heals children: safety first, then stable caregiving, then trauma processing. TF-CBT (Trauma-Focused CBT) adapted for children, play therapy for young ones, and caregiver training all work. The brain's plasticity is the great hope.

points_json.example: A teacher trained in trauma-informed care who responds to a child's outburst with calm curiosity instead of punishment.
points_json.point: Trauma-informed systems matter: schools, foster care, and clinics that understand trauma responses avoid re-traumatizing children. Punishing trauma behaviors deepens them; understanding them heals.

points_json.example: An adult survivor who after years of therapy says: 'It happened to me, but it is not who I am.'
points_json.point: Adult recovery is absolutely possible: trauma-focused therapies, EMDR, and long-term relational healing work at any age. Resilience research shows most traumatized children — with even one stable supportive adult — grow into healthy adults.

summary: How early trauma rewires the growing brain — attachment damage, the biology of toxic stress, why it's misdiagnosed, and what heals children.
title: Childhood Trauma and Development

points_json.example: A 16-year-old girl who weighs 35 kg but cries daily believing she is fat, and runs 2 hours every morning to burn every calorie.
points_json.point: Anorexia Nervosa means severely restricting food with intense fear of weight gain and distorted body image — seeing fat where there is none. It has the highest mortality of any mental disorder, from starvation complications or suicide.

points_json.example: A patient whose heart rate drops to 35 beats per minute and who grows fine body hair (lanugo) as starvation deepens.
points_json.point: Starvation's medical ravages: dangerously low heart rate and blood pressure, bone loss, infertility, hair loss, constant coldness, and electrolyte crashes that can stop the heart. The brain shrinks — and thinking becomes rigid and obsessional.

points_json.example: A girl who cuts food into tiny pieces, eats in secret, and panics if anyone watches her eat.
points_json.point: Behavioral signs: extreme calorie counting, food rituals, excessive exercise, baggy clothes to hide weight loss, lying about eating, and social withdrawal. Families often notice the secrecy before the weight loss.

points_json.example: Two types: restricting (dieting, fasting, over-exercise only) and binge-eating/purging (binges plus vomiting or laxatives).
points_json.point: The restricting type loses weight purely through not eating. The binge-purge type binges then purges — and is often missed because weight may look less extreme. Both share the same core body-image terror.

points_json.example: A perfectionist teen whose whole family diets and whose social media is full of thin-ideal images.
points_json.point: Causes: genetics (highly heritable), perfectionist anxious temperament, dieting (the top trigger — most cases start with a diet), cultural thin ideals, family weight focus, and trauma. Athletes, dancers, and models face higher risk.

points_json.example: In family-based treatment, parents temporarily take charge of all meals until their teenager's weight is restored.
points_json.point: For adolescents, Family-Based Treatment (Maudsley) is the gold standard: parents refeed the child, then gradually return control. For adults, CBT-E and specialist supportive therapy work. No medicine treats anorexia's core — nutrition rehabilitation comes first.

points_json.example: A patient hospitalized at 32 kg who gains steadily on a supervised refeeding plan with heart monitoring.
points_json.point: Medical stabilization: severe cases need hospitalization — refeeding must be gradual to avoid refeeding syndrome (deadly electrolyte shifts). Weight restoration alone improves mood and thinking dramatically.

points_json.example: A recovered woman who still dislikes her thighs but eats normally, works, and laughs with friends.
points_json.point: Recovery is possible but slow: about half recover fully, a third improve partially. Full weight restoration, challenging body-image thoughts, and treating co-occurring anxiety and depression protect against relapse.

summary: Starvation as a disorder — the medical dangers, the two subtypes, why diets trigger it, family-based treatment, and the slow road to recovery.
title: Anorexia Nervosa in Depth

points_json.example: A 7-year-old who eats only white rice and plain bread, and gags at any new food.
points_json.point: ARFID (Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder) means avoiding food from sensory issues (texture, smell), fear of choking or vomiting, or simple lack of interest in eating — causing weight loss or nutrition deficiency, but WITHOUT body-image distortion. This is the key difference from anorexia.

points_json.example: A child who after choking on a grape refuses all solid foods for months.
points_json.point: Three ARFID presentations: sensory sensitivity, fear of aversive consequences (choking, vomiting), and low appetite/interest. It is common in autistic children and anxious temperaments, and often starts in early childhood.

points_json.example: A pregnant woman who craves and eats chalk and clay daily.
points_json.point: Pica is eating non-food items — clay, chalk, paper, soil — for a month or more, beyond cultural or developmental norms. It can signal iron or zinc deficiency, so blood tests come first. It is most common in children, pregnant women, and people with intellectual disability.

points_json.example: A toddler who eats paint chips from old walls — risking lead poisoning.
points_json.point: Pica's dangers are medical: lead poisoning, intestinal blockage, infections, and malnutrition. Treatment must address both the behavior and the medical risks — environmental safety first.

points_json.example: A child who brings food back up and re-chews it daily, like a cow chewing cud.
points_json.point: Rumination Disorder means repeatedly regurgitating food and re-chewing or spitting it out, for a month or more, without nausea or a medical cause. It often follows stress and responds to behavioral treatment.

points_json.example: A boy with ARFID who tries one tiny bite of a new food daily, earning a reward each time.
points_json.point: ARFID treatment: gradual food exposure (tiny steps up a hierarchy), anxiety management for choking fears, sensory desensitization, and family meals without pressure. Appetite stimulants are sometimes used short-term.

points_json.example: A pica patient whose clay-eating stopped after iron supplements corrected her deficiency.
points_json.point: Pica treatment: correct nutritional deficiencies first, then behavioral strategies — keeping non-foods out of reach, teaching alternative behaviors, and rewarding appropriate eating. Most childhood pica fades with age.

points_json.example: Parents taught to offer new foods calmly 15+ times without forcing — because forced feeding worsens ARFID.
points_json.point: The golden rule for all three: never force-feed or punish. Pressure increases avoidance. Calm repeated exposure, medical monitoring, and patience work — force backfires every time.

summary: Eating disorders without body-image fears — ARFID's sensory and fear-based avoidance, pica's non-food cravings, rumination, and gentle treatments.
title: ARFID and Pica in Depth

points_json.example: A 9-year-old who loses his homework daily, cannot sit through a meal, and blurts answers before the teacher finishes.
points_json.point: Childhood ADHD: inattention (careless mistakes, disorganization, forgetfulness) plus hyperactivity-impulsivity (fidgeting, interrupting, excessive talking). Symptoms must appear before age 12, in 2+ settings, and impair functioning — not just high energy.

points_json.example: An inattentive girl who stares out the window all lesson — missed for years because she wasn't disruptive.
points_json.point: Girls are underdiagnosed: they more often show the quiet inattentive type, internalizing struggles as anxiety or 'laziness.' Many women are first diagnosed in adulthood after a lifetime of unexplained difficulty.

points_json.example: A university student with ADHD who failed twice, then thrived with medicine, a coach, and recorded lectures.
points_json.point: Adult ADHD: hyperactivity becomes inner restlessness; inattention becomes lost jobs, missed deadlines, impulsive spending, and relationship conflict. About 60% of childhood cases continue into adulthood — it is not outgrown by most.

points_json.example: A 45-year-old diagnosed after his son's diagnosis — suddenly his whole life makes sense.
points_json.point: Adult diagnosis requires childhood evidence: old report cards, parent interviews. Many adults seek diagnosis after their child's — recognizing their own lifelong patterns for the first time.

points_json.example: An ADHD adult whose untreated symptoms led to job losses, debt, and divorce.
points_json.point: Untreated adult ADHD raises risks: unemployment, substance use, accidents (especially driving), relationship breakdown, and depression. Treatment dramatically lowers all of these — diagnosis is protective.

points_json.example: A child on stimulant medicine sits through class for the first time and finishes his worksheet.
points_json.point: Treatment across ages: stimulants (methylphenidate, amphetamines) are most effective at all ages; behavioral parent training for children; CBT adapted for ADHD, coaching, and workplace accommodations for adults. Exercise and sleep help everyone.

points_json.example: A programmer with ADHD who excels in crisis-mode startups but fails in slow bureaucratic jobs.
points_json.point: Strengths matter: many with ADHD show creativity, hyperfocus on interests, high energy, and crisis resilience. Career fit — stimulating, varied work — matters as much as treatment.

points_json.example: An elderly ADHD patient who finally understands her lifelong 'flakiness' and forgives herself at 70.
points_json.point: ADHD in older adults is newly recognized: lifelong symptoms persist, and stimulants can still help. The greatest gift of late diagnosis is self-compassion — decades of shame reframed as neurology.

summary: ADHD from childhood to old age — why girls are missed, how symptoms transform in adults, the costs of no treatment, and lifespan management.
title: ADHD Across the Lifespan

points_json.example: A child who at age 5 speaks in single words and needs help with dressing and eating.
points_json.point: Intellectual Developmental Disorder (intellectual disability) means significantly below-average intellectual functioning (IQ ~70 or below) PLUS problems with adaptive skills — communication, self-care, daily living. Both must start in childhood. IQ alone never decides the diagnosis.

points_json.example: A man with mild ID who lives semi-independently, works a supported job, but needs help with banking and medical decisions.
points_json.point: Severity levels: mild (most common — can work and live with some support), moderate (needs daily support), severe (needs extensive support), profound (needs constant care). Severity is judged by adaptive functioning, not just IQ scores.

points_json.example: A child with Down syndrome (trisomy 21) — the most common genetic cause.
points_json.point: Causes: genetic conditions (Down syndrome, fragile X), prenatal exposures (alcohol — fetal alcohol syndrome, infections), birth complications (oxygen loss), and childhood factors (severe malnutrition, lead poisoning, brain injury). Many cases have no identified cause.

points_json.example: A mother who drank during pregnancy gives birth to a child with fetal alcohol syndrome.
points_json.point: Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders are a leading PREVENTABLE cause: alcohol in pregnancy can cause intellectual disability, growth problems, and facial features. No safe amount of alcohol in pregnancy is established.

points_json.example: A child with PKU (a metabolic disorder) who develops normally because newborn screening caught it and diet treatment started immediately.
points_json.point: Prevention wins: newborn screening catches treatable metabolic disorders; folic acid prevents neural tube defects; vaccines prevent brain-damaging infections; prenatal care and avoiding alcohol and toxins protect development.

points_json.example: A teenager with moderate ID who learns to cook, use public transport, and work in a café through skills training.
points_json.point: Intervention: early childhood programs, special education, speech and occupational therapy, and adaptive skills training. The goal is maximum independence — every skill learned is freedom gained.

points_json.example: A young woman with mild ID who is taught about consent, safe relationships, and how to report abuse.
points_json.point: Vulnerability: people with ID face high rates of abuse and exploitation. Protection means teaching safety skills, ensuring supervised environments, and believing reports — they are often disbelieved.

points_json.example: A 50-year-old with Down syndrome developing early Alzheimer's — and a family prepared with a care plan.
points_json.point: Lifespan issues: people with Down syndrome age early and face high Alzheimer's risk. Planning covers aging caregivers ('who cares when parents can't?'), health monitoring, and supported decision-making that respects autonomy.

summary: Understanding intellectual disability fully — severity by real-life functioning, preventable causes, early intervention, vulnerability, and lifespan care.
title: Intellectual Disability in Depth

points_json.example: A student who suddenly collapses laughing during a joke, then wakes up minutes later confused.
points_json.point: Narcolepsy means the brain cannot control sleep-wake properly: irresistible daytime sleep attacks plus cataplexy — sudden muscle weakness triggered by strong emotions like laughter or surprise. It is caused by loss of hypocretin (orexin), the brain chemical that keeps us awake.

points_json.example: A narcoleptic driver who falls asleep at a red light — and must surrender his license.
points_json.point: Beyond sleepiness: fragmented night sleep, vivid dream-like hallucinations when falling asleep or waking, and sleep paralysis. Driving and safety-critical jobs become dangerous. Diagnosis needs a sleep study (MSLT) showing rapid entry into dream sleep.

points_json.example: A child with narcolepsy misdiagnosed with laziness for years before a sleep study revealed the truth.
points_json.point: Narcolepsy usually starts in teens but diagnosis takes a decade on average — mistaken for laziness, depression, or epilepsy. An autoimmune attack on hypocretin cells after infections (like H1N1 flu) is a suspected trigger.

points_json.example: A patient on scheduled naps plus stimulant medicine who returns to full-time work.
points_json.point: Treatment: scheduled daytime naps, stimulant medicines for sleepiness, sodium oxybate for cataplexy and night sleep, plus safety planning. There is no cure, but good management restores near-normal life.

points_json.example: A child who sits up screaming in the first hours of sleep, eyes open but unresponsive, remembering nothing in the morning.
points_json.point: NREM parasomnias — sleepwalking, sleep terrors, confusional arousals — happen in deep sleep's first third of the night. The person looks awake but is confused, hard to wake, and forgets everything. They run in families and are common in children.

points_json.example: A sleepwalker who once walked out the front door and was found two streets away.
points_json.point: Safety first for sleepwalking: lock doors and windows, remove hazards, avoid sleep deprivation and alcohol (both trigger episodes). Most children outgrow it; adult onset deserves a sleep study.

points_json.example: An elderly man who punches and shouts in his sleep, sometimes falling out of bed while dreaming he is being chased.
points_json.point: REM Sleep Behavior Disorder: the body fails to stay paralyzed during dreams, so people act dreams out — talking, punching, leaping. In older adults it strongly predicts Parkinson's disease years later — a vital early warning sign.

points_json.example: A patient who cannot move for a minute on waking, terrified, while a shadowy figure seems to sit on her chest.
points_json.point: Sleep paralysis with hypnagogic hallucinations is common and harmless — the brain wakes before the body's sleep paralysis lifts. Knowing what it is removes the terror; irregular sleep schedules make it worse.

summary: When sleep machinery breaks — narcolepsy's hypocretin loss and cataplexy, sleepwalking, night terrors, dream-enacting disorder, and sleep paralysis.
title: Narcolepsy and Parasomnias

points_json.example: A healthy 25-year-old who is convinced every headache is a brain tumor and checks his body for lumps 20 times a day.
points_json.point: Illness Anxiety Disorder (the modern term for hypochondriasis) is intense fear of having a serious disease with little or no actual symptoms. Normal body sensations — a headache, a muscle twitch — are misread as deadly illness. It must last 6+ months.

points_json.example: A woman who has had 8 normal MRIs but remains certain the doctors missed her brain tumor.
points_json.point: Two patterns: care-seeking (endless doctor visits, tests, ER trips) and care-avoidant (terrified of doctors, avoiding all medical care). Both are driven by the same fear — reassurance never lasts, so the cycle repeats.

points_json.example: A man who spends 4 hours daily on medical websites, emerging more terrified each time.
points_json.point: Cyberchondria fuels the disorder: symptom-checking online always finds worst-case matches. Body-checking (probing lymph nodes, mirror-checking moles) and asking family for reassurance are the compulsive behaviors maintaining it.

points_json.example: A patient whose health anxiety exploded after her father's sudden death from a heart attack.
