points_json.point: Triggers: serious illness or death of a loved one, one's own health scare, childhood experiences with sick parents, and anxious temperament. The COVID pandemic caused a worldwide surge in health anxiety.

points_json.example: A sufferer who interprets a normal stomach gurgle as stomach cancer — the catastrophic misinterpretation at the core.
points_json.point: The cognitive model: harmless sensations → catastrophic misinterpretation → anxiety → more body vigilance → more sensations noticed. Selective attention to the body creates the very 'evidence' feared.

points_json.example: A patient who agrees to check her body only twice daily instead of 20 times — anxiety drops within 2 weeks.
points_json.point: CBT is the treatment of choice: reducing body-checking and reassurance-seeking, challenging catastrophic interpretations, exposure to feared situations (hospitals, illness stories), and scheduled 'worry time.' It works as well as medicines.

points_json.example: A doctor who schedules brief monthly check-ups instead of emergency visits — giving safety without feeding the cycle.
points_json.point: Medical management matters: one trusted doctor, scheduled (not symptom-driven) visits, and avoiding unnecessary tests. Doctors must validate the suffering while gently refusing to feed the reassurance cycle.

points_json.example: A recovered patient who feels a chest twinge, notes it calmly, and goes back to work — the feared catastrophe never arriving.
points_json.point: Recovery means tolerating uncertainty about health — accepting that no test guarantees perfect health. Mindfulness of body sensations without reacting, plus treating co-occurring anxiety and depression, keeps gains lasting.

summary: The terror of being seriously ill — care-seeking vs care-avoidant types, the cyberchondria trap, catastrophic misinterpretation, and CBT's way out.
title: Illness Anxiety Disorder in Depth

points_json.example: A woman who suddenly cannot move her legs after a family fight — all scans are normal, and the paralysis fades once the conflict is resolved.
points_json.point: Conversion Disorder (Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder) means real neurological symptoms — paralysis, blindness, seizures, speech loss — with no medical cause found. The person is NOT faking: the brain genuinely produces the symptom, often after stress or trauma.

points_json.example: A soldier who goes blind the night before battle, with perfectly healthy eyes.
points_json.point: Classic examples: functional paralysis, non-epileptic seizures (look like epilepsy but EEG is normal), functional blindness or deafness, and speech problems. Symptoms often symbolically relate to the stress — the soldier 'cannot face' battle.

points_json.example: A patient oddly unconcerned about her sudden paralysis — while her family panics.
points_json.point: La belle indifférence — strange calm about dramatic symptoms — was once thought typical, but it is actually uncommon. Its absence does NOT mean faking. Most patients are appropriately distressed.

points_json.example: A teenager whose functional seizures began after sexual abuse she could not speak about.
points_json.point: Triggers: psychological trauma, physical injury, or illness that becomes a template. The brain's predictive machinery misfires — expecting dysfunction and creating it. Women and adolescents are most affected.

points_json.example: A neurologist who says 'Your tests are normal — this is real, and the brain can unlearn it' — the most therapeutic sentence.
points_json.point: Diagnosis is now positive, not just exclusion: neurologists look for signs of inconsistency (Hoover's sign in leg weakness, normal EEG during seizures) that prove functional origin. A respectful explanation is the first treatment.

points_json.example: A paralyzed patient who walks again after physiotherapy focused on automatic movements, not the 'paralyzed' leg.
points_json.point: Treatment: physiotherapy retraining automatic movement, CBT addressing stress and illness beliefs, and treating co-occurring anxiety, depression, or PTSD. Hypnosis and suggestion techniques have long histories here.

points_json.example: A patient whose seizures stopped after trauma therapy processed the assault behind them.
points_json.point: Address the root: when trauma drives symptoms, trauma-focused therapy resolves them. Family therapy helps when symptoms serve a (unconscious) role in family dynamics — like keeping a fragile family together.

points_json.example: A recovered patient who recognizes early warning signs — numbness under stress — and uses grounding before symptoms bloom.
points_json.point: Prognosis: many recover fully, especially with early treatment. Chronic cases need long-term rehabilitation. Relapses under stress are common — teaching early recognition and coping prevents full return.

summary: Real paralysis with no medical cause — how functional symptoms work, why patients aren't faking, the neurologist's key role, and retraining the brain.
title: Conversion Disorder in Depth

points_json.example: A man who needs a pill every morning to stop shaking and sweating, has lost his job, but keeps using despite his wife's pleas.
points_json.point: Opioid Use Disorder follows the 11 DSM-5-TR criteria — using more than planned, failed quit attempts, cravings, neglected duties, social problems, dangerous use, tolerance, and withdrawal. Severity: 2–3 mild, 4–5 moderate, 6+ severe.

points_json.example: A patient prescribed oxycodone after surgery who within months is buying pills illegally.
points_json.point: How it starts: prescription painkillers are the most common gateway — about 1 in 4 long-term users develop problems. Others start with heroin. Fentanyl's extreme potency has made street opioids far deadlier.

points_json.example: A user in withdrawal: sweating, nausea, diarrhea, muscle cramps, insomnia — like severe flu plus intense craving.
points_json.point: Opioid withdrawal is agonizing but rarely deadly (unlike alcohol withdrawal). It begins 6–12 hours after the last dose and peaks at 2–3 days. Fear of withdrawal is the main reason users keep using.

points_json.example: A first-time user who overdoses because the batch was stronger than expected — breathing slows, then stops.
points_json.point: Overdose kills by suppressing breathing. Naloxone (Narcan) reverses it in minutes and is now available without prescription in many places. Never use alone; fentanyl test strips save lives.

points_json.example: A patient on methadone who holds a steady job and parents normally for the first time in years.
points_json.point: Medication-assisted treatment is the gold standard: methadone (daily clinic), buprenorphine (safer, take-home), and naltrexone (blocks effects). These cut death rates by half or more — they are treatment, not 'replacing one drug with another.'

points_json.example: A user who switches to clean needles and never shares — avoiding HIV and hepatitis while working toward recovery.
points_json.point: Harm reduction saves lives now: needle exchanges, supervised consumption sites, naloxone kits, and fentanyl testing. Abstinence is the goal; survival is the prerequisite.

points_json.example: A recovering patient in CBT who maps her triggers — Friday nights, old friends — and builds new routines.
points_json.point: Psychosocial treatment: CBT for triggers and cravings, contingency management (rewards for clean tests), motivational interviewing, and peer support. Treating co-occurring depression, anxiety, and trauma is essential.

points_json.example: A mother in recovery for 3 years who mentors new patients — proof that remission is real.
points_json.point: Recovery outlook: opioid use disorder is a chronic condition like diabetes — manageable, with relapses part of the course, not failure. Long-term maintenance, stable housing, and supportive relationships predict lasting remission.

summary: The overdose crisis up close — how prescription pills lead to heroin and fentanyl, withdrawal, naloxone, and why medication-assisted treatment saves lives.
title: Opioid Use Disorder

points_json.example: A student who stays awake 3 nights on meth, then crashes into days of depression and paranoia.
points_json.point: Stimulant Use Disorder covers cocaine, methamphetamine, and misused prescription stimulants (Adderall). All flood the brain with dopamine — producing euphoria, energy, and confidence, followed by crashes, paranoia, and compulsive reuse.

points_json.example: A cocaine user whose nasal septum is destroyed and who has had two heart scares by age 30.
points_json.point: Cocaine's dangers: heart attacks, strokes, nasal damage (snorted), lung damage (smoked as crack), and severe paranoia. Crack's rapid intense high makes it among the most addictive forms.

points_json.example: A meth user with rotted teeth ('meth mouth'), skin sores from picking, and extreme weight loss.
points_json.point: Methamphetamine's signature damage: severe dental decay, skin lesions, rapid aging, and psychosis that can mimic schizophrenia — paranoia and hallucinations lasting months after quitting.

points_json.example: A college student selling his Adderall prescription — and another snorting it to study all night.
points_json.point: Prescription stimulant misuse is rising: students use them as 'study drugs,' but non-prescribed use brings addiction, psychosis risk, and heart dangers. They do not actually improve grades in non-ADHD users.

points_json.example: A binge user who hasn't slept in 4 days, convinced the police are outside — stimulant psychosis.
points_json.point: Stimulant psychosis: prolonged use causes paranoid delusions and hallucinations indistinguishable from schizophrenia. It usually clears with abstinence but can persist for months, needing antipsychotic treatment.

points_json.example: A quitter who sleeps 16 hours daily for weeks, eats constantly, and feels no pleasure in anything.
points_json.point: Withdrawal is a crash, not shakes: hypersomnia, increased appetite, deep depression, and intense craving. Suicide risk peaks during this crash — monitoring is critical.

points_json.example: A patient in contingency management who earns vouchers for each clean urine test — and stays clean 3 months straight.
points_json.point: Treatment: no approved medicines yet (unlike opioids), so behavioral treatments lead — contingency management has the strongest evidence, plus CBT, community reinforcement, and treating co-occurring disorders. Long-term follow-up is key.

points_json.example: A former meth user 2 years clean who still avoids old neighborhoods and carries a relapse plan.
points_json.point: Recovery: the brain's dopamine system slowly heals over 1–2 years. Relapse is common — each attempt teaches more. Stable housing, employment, and new social circles are the strongest protectors.

summary: Cocaine, meth, and misused study drugs — the dopamine flood, stimulant psychosis, the crash withdrawal, and the behavioral treatments with the best evidence.
title: Stimulant Use Disorders

points_json.example: A teenager who says 'Everyone would be better off without me' — and has started giving away prized possessions.
points_json.point: Warning signs: talking about death or being a burden, withdrawing, giving things away, sudden calm after depression (may mean a decision was made), increased substance use, and researching methods. Always take every sign seriously.

points_json.example: A clinician who asks directly: 'Are you thinking of killing yourself?' — and the patient finally says yes.
points_json.point: Ask directly — it does NOT plant the idea. This myth costs lives. Direct questions open the door: ask about thoughts, plans, means, intent, and timeline. Vague answers need gentle, persistent follow-up.

points_json.example: A patient with a specific plan, access to pills, and a date — versus one with fleeting thoughts and strong family support.
points_json.point: Risk assessment weighs: plan specificity, access to means, intent strength, past attempts (the top predictor), hopelessness, impulsivity, substance use — against protective factors: supportive relationships, children, faith, future hope, and treatment engagement.

points_json.example: A man who attempted suicide last year, drinks heavily, and just lost his job and wife in the same month.
points_json.point: Highest-risk groups: people with prior attempts, men over 75 and young men, those with depression/bipolar/schizophrenia, substance users, LGBTQ+ youth facing rejection, and recently discharged psychiatric patients.

points_json.example: A family that locks away medicines and firearms after a crisis — cutting risk dramatically.
points_json.point: Means restriction works: most attempts are impulsive — under 10 minutes of thought. Removing or locking lethal means (guns, pills, ropes) saves lives because the impulse passes. This is the single most effective prevention.

points_json.example: A caller to a crisis helpline who stays on the phone for an hour and agrees to go to the emergency room.
points_json.point: Immediate response: never leave a high-risk person alone, call emergency services or crisis lines, create a safety plan (warning signs, coping steps, contacts), and arrange urgent professional follow-up. Listening without judgment matters most.

points_json.example: A patient and therapist who write a safety plan card: 'When I feel hopeless → call Sara → walk to the park → call crisis line.'
points_json.point: Safety planning (Stanley & Brown model): recognize warning signs, use internal coping, contact distracting people/places, ask close others for help, contact professionals, and make the environment safe. It reduces attempts significantly.

points_json.example: A school that teaches students to ask friends directly and tell a trusted adult — and sees help-seeking rise.
points_json.point: Prevention beyond crisis: school programs, responsible media reporting (no method details — the Werther effect is real), treating depression and substance use, reducing stigma, and building belonging. Most suicidal crises pass — help buys time for that.

summary: Saving lives with the right questions — warning signs, how to ask directly, risk vs protective factors, means restriction, and safety planning.
title: Suicide Risk Assessment and Prevention
